common_name: Adams I Elderberry (Adams No. 1, Original Union Springs American Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in well-drained to moderately moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; plant alongside Adams No. 2 or another distinct American elderberry cultivar to improve cross-pollination and fruit set.

directions: Adams No. 1 was one of two wild American elderberry seedlings selected by grower William Adams near Union Springs, New York in the early 1910s and released together in 1926 after an eleven-year evaluation by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station at Geneva. For decades it stood alongside its sibling Adams No. 2 as one of the only named elderberry cultivars available to North American growers, valued for its heavy, dependable cropping and vigorous, upright cane growth rather than for the exceptionally large individual berries that made Adams No. 2 more famous. Broad, flat-topped clusters of white flowers open in June and July, maturing into small dark purple-black berries by late summer that, like all elderberry fruit, must be cooked before eating. Plant it near a genetically distinct cultivar such as Adams No. 2, York, or Nova to boost pollination, and remove the oldest canes each winter to keep the planting productive.
sources: Cornell University — Elderberry Culture in New York State (New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva)
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry — Elderberry Production Guide
Midwest Elderberry Cooperative — Elderberry Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, which develops the deepest purple leaf color; part shade causes the foliage to fade toward green.

directions: Purpurea is one of the older purple-leaved selections of European black elder, predating and giving rise to later, more deeply and stably colored sports such as Guincho Purple. Its new spring growth opens a dusky reddish-purple but tends to soften toward bronzy green as summer heat sets in, especially with any shade, making full sun essential for holding color through the season. Flat clusters of pale pink-tinged flowers open in early summer above the purple-tinted foliage, followed by shiny black berries typical of European elder. Cut the shrub back hard in late winter to renew strongly colored young stems, since older wood produces coarser, less vividly tinted leaves.

common_name: Pyramidalis Elderberry (Columnar Upright European Black Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; its narrow, upright branching habit suits a tight side yard or narrow screen where a wide-spreading elder would not fit.

directions: Pyramidalis is a long-cultivated European elder selection grown for its narrow, upright, densely branched habit, a marked contrast to the broad, arching spread of wild black elder. Flat-topped clusters of creamy white, faintly musky-scented flowers open in early summer along the vertical branches, maturing into the same small black berries as the species, which can be cooked into syrup, wine, or preserves. Because its columnar form is the main feature, it works well as an informal narrow screen or vertical accent where a full-sized elder would overwhelm the space. Prune out any wide-angled or lax shoots as they appear to keep the tight, upright silhouette, and cut back the oldest canes periodically to maintain vigor.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile soil in partial shade, which helps prevent the white leaf variegation from scorching in strong summer sun.

directions: Variegata is an old European elder form marked by irregular creamy-white blotching and marbling scattered across each green leaflet, a bolder and more random pattern than the fine white speckling of Pulverulenta or the neat gold edging of Aureomarginata. Flat clusters of white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small black berries, though the shrub is grown almost entirely for its patterned foliage. It is noticeably less vigorous than green-leaved elder and more prone to leaf scorch, so site it in partial shade with shelter from hot afternoon sun. Watch for and promptly remove any all-green reverted shoots, which grow more strongly than the variegated growth and will gradually overtake the shrub if left in place.

common_name: Plumosa Aurea Elderberry (Golden Cutleaf Red Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where the finely cut golden foliage develops best without scorching in hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plumosa Aurea is the classic old European selection of red elderberry grown for its deeply cut, fern-like foliage that emerges bronze-copper in spring before settling into a bright golden-chartreuse through summer. It is the older parent-type behind later, more sun- and heat-tolerant selections such as Sutherland Gold, and tends to need more reliable afternoon shade to avoid leaf scorch than those improved offspring. Flat clusters of creamy spring flowers mature into small, bright red berries that feed songbirds, though as with all red elderberry the raw fruit and other plant parts are toxic and unsuitable for people to eat uncooked. Prune back hard in late winter to renew the most finely cut, brightly colored foliage, since color and dissection are best on vigorous young growth.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; its low, dense mound of thread-fine foliage suits a rock garden or the front of a shaded border rather than a typical shrub border position.

directions: Tenuifolia is a dwarf, low-mounding selection of red elderberry grown for its extremely finely divided, thread-like green leaflets, giving the whole plant a soft, textural quality more reminiscent of a Japanese maple cultivar or fine-leaved fern than a typical elder. It stays much smaller and denser than the species or gold-leaved selections like Plumosa Aurea and Sutherland Gold, making it a good choice for a rock garden, shaded foundation planting, or anywhere a full-sized elderberry would be out of scale. Small clusters of creamy flowers in spring are followed by red berries in a good year, though the shrub is grown chiefly for its fine foliage texture rather than fruit. Give it consistently moist, humus-rich soil and some afternoon shade, and prune lightly in late winter only to remove dead or crossing stems, since heavy pruning sacrifices the dense, twiggy habit that shows off the foliage best.
